title: The AOL Greeting That Made the Internet Feel Personal
description: How a $200 living room recording and a screeching dial-up modem turned AOL into the front door of the internet for a generation of Americans.
image: Dial-Up Dreams in a Cozy Bedroom.png
alt: A woman using an AOL dial-up desktop computer in a warmly lit bedroom
sections: For a long stretch of the 1990s, going online did not start with a tap or a click. It started with waiting. Someone in the house had to be off the phone, the modem had to dial, and then came a short burst of beeps, hisses, and static that sounded like a robot trying to sing through a kazoo. If the connection held, a friendly male voice would greet you with two simple words, Welcome, and then, if you were lucky, three more that could change the mood of an entire room. You have got mail. That greeting belonged to America Online, known everywhere as AOL, and for millions of people it was not a sound effect. It was the internet itself announcing that it had arrived in their home. Long before push notifications, unread badges, and lock screens crowded with alerts, that one cheerful sentence carried all the excitement of modern messaging in a single moment. Someone, somewhere, had thought of you, written to you, and sent that message across a network you could barely picture, and it was waiting.
A Voice Recorded on a Cassette in a Living Room

The most famous voice of the early internet was never recorded in a famous studio. In 1989, Steve Case, the chief executive of Quantum Computer Services, wanted to add a human voice to the company Quantum Link online service. Quantum would later become America Online. Karen Edwards, who worked as a customer service representative, overheard the conversation and suggested her husband, Elwood Edwards, a professional broadcaster with years of work in radio and television. Edwards sat down in his living room with a cassette recorder and recorded a short set of phrases, Welcome, You have got mail, File is done, and Goodbye, along with a few related lines that followed later. He was paid 200 dollars for the session. There was no way to know in that room, with that modest equipment, that the recording would be heard hundreds of millions of times, or that Edwards later estimated it was being heard more than 35 million times a day at its height. That origin story matters because it captures the scale of what followed. The internet that most Americans first met grew out of ordinary rooms and small decisions that turned out to be enormous. A broadcaster helping out through his wife, a cassette tape, and a company trying to sound less like a machine added up to a voice that made the unfamiliar experience of checking an electronic inbox feel personal. Edwards died on November 5, 2024, one day before his 75th birthday, and the obituaries that followed read less like notices for a voice actor and more like farewells to an era.

Part of the power of that greeting was that getting online used to be an event. Dial-up tied up the household telephone line, so a session online meant no calls in or out. Families negotiated time the way they negotiated the television remote. Teenagers learned to listen for a parent picking up an extension, because that small click could end the connection, and parents learned that a busy signal all evening meant someone was deep in a chat room. Speed shaped everything. Dial-up topped out at 56 kilobits per second, a fraction of what a modern phone connection handles without anyone noticing. A photograph could appear slowly, line by line, slowly revealing itself from the top down. Downloading a song was a commitment. Leaving the computer alone while a file crept toward completion became a normal part of life, and the File is done announcement that Edwards also recorded carried its own small celebration. Because connecting took effort, being connected felt deliberate. People planned sessions. They checked email, visited a handful of favorite places, posted in a forum, and signed off so the phone would be free again. The Goodbye that Edwards recorded at the end of a session was not just politeness. It marked a real leaving, a return to the offline house, the ringing phone, and the rest of the evening.
A Walled Garden That Felt Like a Town

AOL did more than provide a connection. It provided a place. Once inside, members found email, chat rooms organized by interest, instant messaging through AIM, news, games, and guided areas that sorted the sprawling web into something a newcomer could walk through without a map. Critics later called it a walled garden, and the description was fair, but for a first time user in 1995 or 1998, a garden with paths was far less frightening than an open wilderness. Screen names became part of that culture. People chose handles that hid their legal names and announced their humor, their hobbies, or their teenage sense of drama. The anonymity was imperfect and sometimes rowdy, but it also gave shy people a way to speak, gave far flung hobbyists a way to find each other, and gave families in different states a cheap, cheerful way to stay in daily contact that letters and long distance calls never quite matched. The company spread through one of the most visible marketing efforts of the decade, a flood of free trial disks and later CDs that arrived in mailboxes, magazines, and cereal boxes. At its peak around 2000, AOL counted about 25 million subscribers, and by some accounts more than 26 million, and it carried a huge share of the consumer internet traffic in the United States. For a time, asking whether someone was online often meant asking whether they were on AOL. The phrase reached its pop culture peak in 1998, when the film You Have Got Mail, starring Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan, built a romantic comedy around two rival booksellers falling for each other through anonymous AOL messages. The movie works as a time capsule today, with its bookstore wars and its modem sounds, but it also shows how completely the service had entered everyday language. A notification sound had become a movie title that needed no explanation.
The Long Fade and the Final Goodbye

Broadband changed the bargain. Cable and DSL connections stayed on all day, freed the phone line, and made the old ritual of dialing, waiting, and signing off feel like a chore from another life. The walled garden also mattered less as the open web grew easier to navigate and search engines guided people directly to what they wanted. AOL merged with Time Warner in 2000 in a deal that became a symbol of the dot com boom and its excesses, and the company passed through several owners in the years that followed, including Verizon, before landing with Apollo Global Management in 2021 as part of Yahoo. AIM shut down in 2017, closing the instant messaging service that had shaped how a generation typed, abbreviated, and set away messages like diary entries. Dial-up, remarkably, hung on far longer. As recently as 2023, Census estimates counted about 163,000 households in the United States still relying on dial-up, many in places where faster service remained unavailable or unaffordable. Nostalgia was only part of the story. For those households, the modem handshake was not a memory, it was still the only road in. On September 30, 2025, AOL discontinued its dial-up service for good, retiring the AOL Dialer software and the AOL Shield browser along with it, after more than three decades. The company described the move as a routine product evaluation, which is a quiet way to close a loud chapter. The screech that once filled living rooms will now survive mainly in recordings, museum pieces, and the muscle memory of anyone who ever held their breath waiting for a connection to catch.

It is tempting to treat the whole era as a joke about slow speeds and free CDs turned into coasters, and plenty of those jokes are affectionate and earned. Yet something real was learned in those years, and it was learned through sound and ritual as much as through technology. AOL taught people to expect a message to be waiting, to feel a small lift at an alert, to build an identity around a screen name, and to think of a network as a social place rather than a technical one. Modern notifications reflect some of the same design principles: signaling attention, rewarding anticipation, and making a digital action feel immediate. The banners, pings, and badges that compete for attention today are descendants of a friendlier, slower announcement that arrived only after a household negotiation and a modem song. The difference is that the old greeting felt like news from a person, while many new alerts feel like demands from a system. That contrast may be why the clip still circulates whenever the early internet is remembered. People are not only nostalgic for a voice. They are nostalgic for a time when hearing from the online world felt rare enough to celebrate, and simple enough to understand, three words at a time.

title: The Day Digital Design Let Go of Leather and Wood
description: How leather stitching, wooden shelves and yellow legal pads gave way to flat color in 2013, and why designers still argue about what was lost.
alt: Early and modern iPhones showing textured skeuomorphic icons beside contemporary flat icons
sections: Open an early iPhone in your memory and the screen feels like a desk viewed from above. The Notes app is a yellow legal pad with ruled lines. The calendar looks like a page torn from a paper planner. A bookshelf made of polished wood holds your digital books, a stitched leather border frames your contacts, and a green felt table waits inside a games app as if a tiny casino had been folded into the phone. Nothing on that screen admits that it is made of light. Everything insists that it is made of something else. That style had a name that most users never heard until it was already disappearing, skeuomorphism, a long word for a simple idea. A digital object keeps the look of an older physical object so that people recognize what it is for. A trash can means delete because offices had trash cans. A floppy disk means save because saving once meant writing to a floppy disk. A notepad means notes because paper came first. Then, in a single update in 2013, Apple scraped the leather, the felt, and the wood grain off its phones, and the icons stopped pretending.
Why the First Phones Dressed Up as Desks

The disguise was not foolishness. When the first iPhone launched in 2007, the touchscreen was the strange part. Most people had pressed physical buttons all their lives, and a smooth sheet of glass gave no hint about where to push or what would happen next. Making a button look raised, shiny, and pressable answered a question that new users had not yet learned to ask out loud. Making a calendar resemble a calendar meant no manual was required for the first lesson. Apple leaned into that comfort with unusual enthusiasm. Steve Jobs favored the approach, and Scott Forstall, the senior vice president in charge of iOS software, became its most visible champion inside the company. Textures grew richer with each release. By the time iOS 6 and OS X Mountain Lion arrived around 2012, commentators were pointing at stitched leather, linen backgrounds, and wooden shelves as evidence that the imitation had become a habit, and in some corners a joke. The software on a milled aluminum device of remarkable restraint was decorated like a station wagon from another decade. Other designers followed, as designers tended to follow Apple. Materials that had no reason to exist on a screen, glass reflections on icons for apps that contained no glass, pages that curled for readers who had never asked for curling pages, spread across phones and websites. A metaphor that began as a courtesy to beginners hardened into a fashion, and fashion, once everyone wears it, starts to look like a uniform.
The Shakeup That Cleared the Desk

The turn came from a change in people before it came as a change in pixels. Forstall left Apple in the management shakeup of late 2012, following the troubled launch of Apple Maps and long reported clashes with other executives. Design chief Jony Ive, who had shaped the hardware and favored spare, industrial minimalism, took responsibility for the human interface work as well, uniting how the device looked with how its software behaved. At the Worldwide Developers Conference on June 10, 2013, Apple unveiled iOS 7, and the audience saw the most sweeping visual redesign the iPhone had ever received. The wood, felt, and leather were gone. Icons were redrawn as flat shapes in bright color, type thinned down, buttons lost their heavy shading and became simple text or fine outlines, and translucent layers floated over content with a soft blur, giving depth through stacking rather than through fake materials. Ive said at the time that people had become comfortable touching glass and no longer needed the physical world referenced so literally, a remark that Apple Insider and others have returned to often in retellings of the period. Reaction split immediately. Admirers called the new look clean, modern, and honest, a screen that finally admitted it was a screen. Critics called the early version of iOS 7 harsh, unfinished, and confusing, pointing at thin type that was hard to read and icons that looked, to some eyes, like they had been drawn for children. Forbes declared the death of skeuomorphism, and across the industry the obituary doubled as a starting gun. Google moved toward its own Material Design language in 2014, Microsoft had already bet on flat tiles with Windows Phone and Windows 8, and app makers everywhere flattened their icons, palettes, and buttons in the months that followed.
What Flat Design Gave, and What It Quietly Took

The case for flat design was never only about taste. Simpler visual elements could be easier to adapt across screen sizes that multiplied every year, and calmer to look at on devices people now consulted hundreds of times a day. A leather texture that charmed on one phone size could look muddy on another. A simple shape held up. As phones became the main computer for most of the world, that kind of adaptability stopped being a preference and started being infrastructure. Something was traded away in the exchange, and the argument about that trade has never really ended. Critics of pure flatness noticed that when every button loses its shading and every surface loses its shadow, people can have trouble telling what can be tapped from what is merely decoration. Designers began smuggling depth back in, a soft shadow here, a raised card there, until the flat era quietly admitted that human eyes like clues. Later styles with names like neumorphism tried, with mixed success, to push soft, extruded shapes back onto the screen, proof that the pendulum had energy in both directions. There is also the matter of memory. The old icons carried a shared visual vocabulary built over a century of desks, offices, and kitchens. A generation that has never mailed a film roll or wound a cassette still recognizes the envelopes, cameras, and reels those icons borrowed, yet the borrowing grows stranger every year. The floppy disk survives as the universal symbol for saving files among people who have never held one, which suggests that a skeuomorph, once learned, can outlive the object it copied by decades. Flat design did not erase that inheritance. It froze parts of it in place, simplified into glyphs whose origins grow more mysterious with each new class of first graders handed a tablet.

Look closely at a current phone and the great war of 2013 reads less like a victory than like a truce. Icons are flat in outline but shaded with gentle gradients. Cards float with real shadows. Apples recent design languages play with translucency and light in ways that would have surprised the strictest flat era purists, while stopping well short of stitching digital leather onto anything. The materials are imaginary now, glass and glow rather than wood and felt, but they are materials all the same. Screens keep inventing substances because people keep reading substance as meaning. That may be the real story underneath the style fight. Skeuomorphism belonged to a moment when the digital world needed a passport from the physical one. Flat design belonged to the moment after, when the digital world felt established enough to travel on its own papers. Neither moment ended the human habit of asking an unfamiliar thing to resemble a familiar one. The habit only changed its costume, from a wooden bookshelf to a floating pane of frosted glass, and it will change again when the next unfamiliar surface, perhaps one worn on the face or projected into a room, needs to teach strangers where to look and what to touch. The icons on a home screen look modest, but they record that whole negotiation in miniature. A yellow pad became a white rectangle with lines, then lines alone, each step trusting the user a little more and explaining itself a little less. Whether that trust reads as progress or as loss depends on where a person started. Someone who learned touchscreens through stitched leather remembers a kindness in it. Someone who arrived later sees only clutter that mercifully cleared. Both are looking at the same small squares, and both, in their own way, are right.

title: Before the Feed, the Comment Section Was the Conversation
description: Long before feeds and followers, readers argued, joked and built reputations under articles. A look at the rise, fall and quiet return of comments.
alt: A laptop displaying a personal Los Angeles sunset blog and reader comments on a nostalgic desk
sections: Scroll to the bottom of an old blog post that still allows replies and you can feel a familiar atmosphere in an unfamiliar place. Strangers are performing for each other. Regulars greet each other by username. Someone has arrived with a correction, someone else with a grudge, and a third person has written a reply longer and better sourced than the article above it. Likes, follows, pile ons, running jokes, reputations built one post at a time, all of it is there, humming along years before most of those readers had ever heard the phrase social media. Comment sections were among the places where the public web practiced large scale social conversation. Letters to the editor had always existed, but they moved at the speed of print, passed through an editors hands, and appeared days later, trimmed and tamed. A comment appeared in minutes, under your chosen name, in front of everyone. For readers who had grown up consuming media in silence, that small text box at the bottom of a page was a genuinely new civic experience, a chance to answer back in public and be answered in return.
From Guest Books to the Bottom of Every Page

The habits formed early. Personal sites in the 1990s kept guest books where visitors signed their names and left a line of praise or mischief. Forums and message boards gathered people around shared obsessions, from car repair to obscure bands, and taught the grammar that comment sections inherited, threaded replies, quoted passages, moderators with quiet power, and regulars whose posting history functioned as a biography. When blogs took off in the early 2000s, they carried that culture into publishing itself. A post was understood to be the start of a conversation, not the end of one, and a blogger with a lively comment thread had something no print columnist could buy, a room that stayed full after the author left it. News organizations arrived more cautiously and then all at once. Commenting promised engagement, return visits, and pages that kept growing after publication, and in an era when publishers were anxious about losing readers to the open web, a busy thread looked like loyalty made visible. Readers corrected errors, added local knowledge no reporter could have gathered alone, and sometimes argued a story into a better shape in public. Journalists who dove into their own threads, as Washington Post writer Chris Cillizza did on his political blog The Fix beginning in 2006, found devoted communities waiting there, at least at first. The same openness carried the seeds of the sections reputation. Anonymity, or the lighter shield of a pseudonym, lowered the cost of cruelty. Threads on hard stories attracted insults, conspiracy theories, and organized provocation. Research began to suggest that the damage was not confined to hurt feelings. A widely cited study led by Dominique Brossard and Dietram Scheufele at the University of Wisconsin Madison found that uncivil comments under a balanced article about nanotechnology polarized readers and shifted how they judged the risks described in the article itself. The conversation below the line, as British journalists came to call it, could quietly rewrite the story above it.
The Years When Publishers Walked Away

Popular Science made the break impossible to ignore. On September 24, 2013, the magazine announced that it would no longer accept comments on new articles, declaring plainly that comments can be bad for science. Online editor Suzanne LaBarre pointed to trolls and spambots, and to research showing that a fractious minority could skew a readers perception of solid reporting. A publication devoted to evidence had concluded that the evidence about its own comment section pointed in one direction, and it closed the door. Popular Science was early, but it was not alone for long. In a concentrated season of retreat, Reuters, Recode, Mic, The Week, and the Chicago Sun Times all shut or sharply reduced their comment sections in and around 2014, and many editors gave the same pair of reasons. Moderation consumed staff time and money that shrinking newsrooms believed belonged in reporting, and the conversation, they argued, had already moved. Readers were discussing stories on Facebook and Twitter, platforms that promised larger audiences and, at the time, an appealing story about someone else handling the ugliest parts of the job. NPR joined the departures on August 17, 2016, ending comments on its site after eight years and explaining that a tiny fraction of its audience produced the overwhelming bulk of its comments, with discussion thriving instead across its many social accounts. Gannett later closed comments across most of its local publications, describing sections that quickly devolve when left unmonitored. By one scholarly count cited in research on United States newspapers, at least 68 outlets closed comment sections between 2008 and the early 2020s. A feature that had once been sold as the democratic future of media had become, in the language of managers, a reputational hazard and a cost center.
What Was Lost in the Move to the Feed

Handing the conversation to social platforms solved a staffing problem and created a subtler one. On a publishers own site, a comment lives beside the work it answers, and the community that forms there belongs, in some meaningful sense, to that publication and its readers. In a feed, the discussion scatters. It is sorted by systems built to reward heat, detached from the article within hours, and addressed to followers rather than to fellow readers who arrived by the same road. Writers kept the insults, since feeds supplied plenty, and lost the regulars, the corrections desk that never slept, and the quiet reader who only ever spoke in that one room. Former defenders of the sections have been candid about the trade. Comment threads, at their best, taught writers things, surfaced errors that editors missed, and gave a publication a public that talked back in its own accent rather than in the flattened tone of a platform. At their worst, they mirrored everything people dislike about feeds, the baiting, the monologues, the handful of voices dominating every subject. The honest history holds both. The comment section was not a golden age ruined by a few bad actors. It was the original laboratory where the internet learned, in public, how hard it is for strangers to talk well at scale, and every social platform since has rerun those experiments with bigger budgets and similar results. The closures also revealed something about how media companies understood their readers. A comment section treats the audience as participants in a shared place. A feed treats the audience as distribution. Walking away from the first in favor of the second made a certain business sense in the middle of the 2010s, when social traffic looked endless, but it rested on rented ground, and publishers learned in later years how quickly a platform can change its terms, its algorithm, or its appetite for news.
The Quiet Return, Behind a Paywall

The most interesting recent chapter is not a restoration but a reinvention. In late 2024, The Washington Post relaunched commenting for subscribers with promises of meaningful, high quality discourse. Wired presented a new commenting experience as part of its subscription offering, a place where readers could connect with writers. The Financial Times has invested in automated moderation that nudges discussions toward substance and draws in readers who rarely comment. In this new model, the comment section is no longer a free town square bolted onto the bottom of an article. It is a members room, part of what a subscription buys, moderated with better tools and, crucially, with a business reason to keep it civil and alive. That shift would have puzzled the bloggers of 2004, for whom openness was the entire point. Yet it also concedes what the closure era tried to deny, that readers value talking where they read, and that a well kept conversation is worth paying to maintain. The technology of moderation has changed too. Automated systems that once strained to catch crude profanity now sort tone, flag bad faith patterns, and surface strong comments that human moderators might never have reached in time. Whether the members room version can recover the democratic messiness that made the original sections matter is an open argument, and it is a fitting one. The comment section began as the webs first experiment in giving readers a microphone, grew into a burden publishers were relieved to surrender, and returned as a product feature once its absence started costing loyalty. Through every phase, the underlying desire never moved. People finish reading something that moved them, angered them, or taught them something, and they want to say so to other people who just read the same words. Platforms rise and collapse around that desire. The small text box at the bottom of the page was simply the first place it found a home.
